college.stem: A person explains a concept fluently while studying with a friend but, a week later, cannot bring it to mind when asked a direct question. Keeping encoding, storage, and retrieval distinct, which conclusion is justified?
options: The recall failure fits a retrieval problem, but this single observation cannot by itself show which memory operation broke down.
The recall failure proves encoding never happened, because information that was encoded will always come back whenever it is needed.
The recall failure proves the information was erased from storage, because anything still held in storage can always be accessed on demand.
The recall failure rules out a retrieval problem, because retrieval is the step that converts new input into a form suitable for storage.
college.why: Encoding converts input into a usable form, storage holds it, and retrieval takes it back out; one failure to recall is consistent with a retrieval problem but does not pinpoint which step failed. The distractors wrongly treat encoded or stored information as always accessible, or confuse retrieval with encoding.

simple.stem: In memory, what does retrieval mean?
options: Taking information back out of memory storage when it is needed.
Converting new information into a usable form so it can be stored.
Holding information in memory over a period of time.
Repeating information silently so it stays in mind longer.
simple.why: Retrieval is taking memories out of storage. Converting information into a usable form is encoding, holding it is storage, and silent repetition is maintenance rehearsal.

college.stem: Episodic and semantic memory are both branches of declarative long-term memory on the memory tree. Which statement correctly matches each one to the kind of content it holds?
options: Episodic memory holds personally experienced events, while semantic memory holds general facts and knowledge.
Episodic memory holds general facts and world knowledge, while semantic memory holds personally experienced events.
Episodic memory holds practiced motor skills, while semantic memory holds brief echoes of recent sounds.
Episodic memory holds fleeting visual images, while semantic memory holds phone numbers being repeated.
college.why: Episodic memory stores events a person experienced (Tulving's “mental time travel”), and semantic memory stores knowledge of facts. The second option reverses the two; motor skills are procedural memory, and brief visual or auditory traces belong to sensory memory.

simple.stem: What kind of information does episodic memory hold?
options: Memories of specific events that you experienced.
General facts and knowledge about the world around you.
Learned motor skills, such as how to ride a bike.
Very brief copies of sights and sounds just sensed.
simple.why: Episodic memory is memory for personally experienced events, a kind of mental time travel. General facts are semantic memory, skills are procedural memory, and brief sensory copies are sensory memory.

college.stem: In Atkinson and Shiffrin's (1968) modal model, a person looks up a phone number, repeats it to themselves, and later recalls it without looking again. Which statement correctly separates the model's memory stores from its control processes?
options: Sensory, short-term, and long-term memory are the stores; attending to and rehearsing the number are control processes acting on it.
Attention, rehearsal, and retrieval are the three stores; sensory and long-term memory are processes that move the number between them.
Sensory memory permanently stores the whole directory, and rehearsal only decides which entry is currently visible to the person.
Short-term memory holds only incoming sensory input, so recalling a previously learned number must bypass short-term memory entirely.
college.why: The modal model has three stores (sensory, short-term, long-term) plus control processes such as attention and rehearsal; retrieval can bring long-term information back into short-term memory. The distractors swap stores and processes or give sensory memory a permanence it lacks.

simple.stem: Atkinson and Shiffrin's (1968) modal model divides memory into which three stores?
options: Sensory memory, short-term memory, and long-term memory, in that order.
Encoding, storage, and retrieval, each holding a different kind of information.
Episodic, semantic, and procedural memory, each lasting about 20 seconds.
Iconic, echoic, and working memory, all lasting less than one second.
simple.why: The modal model's three stores are sensory, short-term, and long-term memory. Encoding, storage, and retrieval are memory operations, and episodic, semantic, and procedural are kinds of long-term memory.

college.stem: While scanning a long list of numbers, a person singles out one number and then repeats it under their breath until they finish dialing. In modal-model terms, which pairing matches each action with the process it reflects?
options: Singling out the number reflects attention, and repeating it until dialing reflects maintenance rehearsal.
Singling out the number reflects maintenance rehearsal, and repeating it until dialing reflects attention.
Singling out the number reflects procedural learning, and repeating it until dialing reflects sensory registration.
Singling out the number reflects retroactive interference, and repeating it until dialing reflects elaborative rehearsal.
college.why: Selecting one item for further processing is attention, and repeating it without adding meaning is maintenance rehearsal. The second option swaps the two, and the last mislabels plain repetition as elaborative rehearsal.

simple.stem: You pick one phone number out of a list and keep repeating it until you dial. What is the repeating called?
options: Maintenance rehearsal, which keeps the number active in short-term memory.
Elaborative rehearsal, which links the number to things you already know.
Retroactive interference, which pushes older phone numbers out of memory.
Sensory memory, which holds an exact copy of the number for years.
simple.why: Repeating information over and over to keep it in short-term memory is maintenance rehearsal. Elaborative rehearsal would link the number to existing knowledge, which simple repetition does not do.

college.stem: A person dials a number they memorized last month by bringing it to mind and holding it there while pressing the keys. Which statement about the modal model fits this situation?
options: Information can be retrieved from long-term memory back into short-term memory, where it is held for immediate use.
Information flows only from sensory to short-term to long-term memory, so a number learned earlier cannot become active again.
The number must have stayed in sensory memory for the whole month in order to guide the person's dialing now.
Retrieving the number erases the difference between short-term and long-term memory, since both now serve one function.
college.why: In the modal model, retrieval brings a number from long-term memory back into short-term memory, where it is remembered long enough to make the call. Flow is not one-way, sensory memory lasts less than a second, and interaction between stores does not make them identical.

simple.stem: In the modal model, what happens when you remember an old phone number to call it again?
options: The number is retrieved from long-term memory back into short-term memory.
The number moves out of short-term memory and back into sensory memory.
The number is encoded again from scratch, as if it were never seen.
The number stays in long-term memory and never enters short-term memory.
simple.why: Retrieval moves the number from long-term memory back into short-term memory so it can be used. Information does not flow back into sensory memory, and the number must be active in short-term memory to guide dialing.

college.stem: Sensory memory includes both an icon and an echo. Which statement correctly characterizes each of them?
options: An icon is a fleeting visual image, and an echo is a brief continuation of a sound in the auditory system.
An icon is a brief continuation of a sound in the auditory system, and an echo is a fleeting visual image.
An icon is a personally experienced episode, and an echo is a general fact stored in long-term memory.
An icon is repetition that keeps information active, and an echo is linking new information to prior knowledge.
college.why: An icon is a brief visual sensory trace and an echo is a brief auditory one. The second option swaps the modalities; the others describe long-term memory types or rehearsal, not sensory memory.

simple.stem: What is an echo in sensory memory?
options: A brief continuation of a sound in the auditory system.
A fleeting visual image that remains after a picture disappears.
A memory of a sound that is kept in storage for many years.
Repeating a word aloud to keep it in short-term memory.
simple.why: An echo is the brief continuation of a sound in the auditory system. A fleeting visual image is an icon, and sensory traces last well under a second, not years.

college.stem: A researcher wants to test Sperling's (1960) claim that more of a briefly flashed letter array is available at first than participants can report before it fades. Which design best tests this claim?
options: Compare whole report with report of one randomly chosen row signaled right after the display ends, with exposure time held constant.
Compare whole report with report of one row identified before the display, so participants can focus on just that row during the exposure.
Compare whole report after a brief exposure with partial report after a much longer exposure, changing both time and task at once.
Compare people who name the whole array with people who copy one row while the letters remain visible on the screen.
college.why: A row cue given after the display ends samples information that was already registered, without letting participants choose a row in advance. An advance cue allows selective encoding, unequal exposure adds a confound, and copying a visible display does not test memory.

simple.stem: In Sperling's (1960) partial report method, what did participants do?
options: After the letters flashed, they heard a tone telling them which row to report.
Before the letters flashed, they were told which single row to memorize.
They reported as many letters as they could from the entire display.
They copied one row of letters while the display stayed on the screen.
simple.why: In partial report, a tone after the letter array told participants which row to report. Reporting the whole display is the whole report method, and an advance cue was not part of the procedure.

college.stem: In Sperling's (1960) study, whole report yielded about 4.5 of 12 letters, yet when a tone right after the display signaled a row, participants reported about 3.3 of that row's 4 letters. What does this comparison best support?
options: More letters were available at first than whole report captured, since most of whichever row was cued could be reported.
Only about 4.5 letters were ever registered, since whole report directly measures everything available right after exposure.
All twelve letters were transferred into long-term memory, since accurate partial report shows permanent storage of the array.
Only the cued row was registered during the display, since a tone played afterward determines where attention was beforehand.
college.why: High partial report for whichever row is cued implies that most of the array was briefly available, followed by rapid loss. It does not show permanent storage, and a cue that comes after the display cannot direct attention during it.

simple.stem: In Sperling's (1960) partial report method, about how many letters of the cued row did participants report?
options: About 3.3 of the 4 letters in the cued row, or 82%.
About 4.5 of the 12 letters in the whole display, or 37.5%.
About 1.5 of the 4 letters in the cued row, or 37.5%.
All 4 letters in the cued row every time, or 100%.
simple.why: With an immediate tone, participants reported about 3.3 of 4 letters (82%) from any cued row. About 4.5 of 12 (37.5%) was the whole report result.

college.stem: In a follow-up to Sperling (1960), the letter display and the cued row stay the same, but the delay before the tone varies. Which result would most directly support a rapidly fading sensory trace?
options: Partial-report accuracy drops as the tone is delayed and nears whole-report levels, even though exposure time is unchanged.
Partial-report accuracy improves when the display is shown for longer, while the tone delay stays the same in every condition.
Whole-report accuracy differs between groups given different instructions beforehand, with no change in the tone delay.
Participants copy the cued row accurately while the letters stay visible, no matter how long they wait before copying.
college.why: Varying only the tone delay isolates how long the trace lasts before a row can be selected; a decline toward whole-report levels shows rapid fading. The other outcomes change exposure or instructions, or let participants see the letters directly.

simple.stem: In Sperling's (1960) delayed partial report condition, what happened as the tone came later after the display?
options: People reported fewer letters, close to whole-report levels.
People reported more letters from the cued row than with no delay.
People reported every letter in the cued row without any errors.
People's accuracy stayed the same across all of the different delays.
simple.why: As the tone was delayed, partial-report accuracy fell, and by about one second it was close to whole-report performance. This shows that sensory memory fades very quickly.

college.stem: Someone claims that Sperling's (1960) whole-report result proves visual sensory memory holds only four or five letters. What is the strongest objection to this claim?
options: Naming letters takes time, so the rest can fade before being reported; immediate partial report shows more was available at first.
Whole report must measure long-term memory, since any spoken report depends on permanent storage rather than a sensory trace.
The partial-report tone adds letters to the display, so the whole-report and partial-report conditions cannot fairly be compared.
The result shows sensory capacity is unlimited, since reporting one row accurately guarantees accurate report of every row.
college.why: People can report only four or five items before the trace decays, but partial report shows the whole scene was encoded at first. The claim confuses how much can be reported with how much was initially available; it does not follow that capacity is unlimited or storage permanent.

simple.stem: What did Sperling (1960) conclude about visual sensory memory?
options: It has a large capacity, but the information in it decays very fast.
It has a small capacity of four or five items and decays slowly.
It has a small capacity, and the information in it lasts for years.
It has a large capacity, and the information in it never decays.
simple.why: Sperling concluded that sensory memory has a large capacity but fast decay, with most of it gone within about one second. The four-or-five-item limit reflects what can be reported before decay, not what was encoded.

college.stem: Two people study an unfamiliar term for equal time. One spells it over and over; the other works out how it relates to ideas they already know. How are these strategies best labeled?
options: The first is mainly maintenance rehearsal; the second is elaborative rehearsal because it links the term to existing knowledge.
The first is mainly elaborative rehearsal; the second is maintenance rehearsal because existing knowledge blocks new encoding.
Both are maintenance rehearsal, because any deliberate study is defined by its repetition rather than by the links it builds.
Both rely on sensory persistence, because keeping attention on the term removes any need for short-term control processes.
college.why: Maintenance rehearsal repeats information; elaborative rehearsal connects it to knowledge in long-term memory. Spending equal time does not make the two strategies the same, and neither relies on sensory memory.

simple.stem: What is elaborative rehearsal?
options: Linking new information to knowledge already stored in long-term memory.
Repeating information silently to keep it in short-term memory.
Holding an exact sensory copy of information for under a second.
Forgetting older information because newer information gets in the way.
simple.why: Elaborative rehearsal links new information with existing knowledge in long-term memory and is a good way to transfer it there. Silent repetition is maintenance rehearsal.

college.stem: Research on short-term memory focuses on two issues, duration and capacity. Which statement correctly defines both and names the process that tends to extend each?
options: Duration is how long information stays in memory, extended by rehearsal; capacity is how much fits at once, extended by chunking.
Duration is how much fits in memory at once, extended by chunking; capacity is how long information stays there, extended by rehearsal.
Duration is how many items are retrieved, extended by interference; capacity is how many items are shown, extended by decay.
Duration is repetition without meaning, extended by encoding; capacity is linking to knowledge, extended by retrieval.
college.why: Duration is how long things stay in memory, and rehearsal seems to extend it; capacity is how many things fit at a time, and chunking seems to extend it. The second option swaps the two definitions.

simple.stem: In short-term memory, what does capacity refer to?
options: How many things can fit in memory at one time.
How long information stays in memory before fading.
How quickly information can be pulled out of memory.
How well new information links to older knowledge.
simple.why: Capacity is how many things fit in memory at a time. How long information stays is duration.

college.stem: In the task used by Brown (1958) and Peterson and Peterson (1959), participants receive three letters and a number, then count backward by threes from that number before recalling the letters. What is the counting task for?
options: It keeps participants from repeating the letters during the delay, so retention can be measured without maintenance rehearsal.
It turns the letters into meaningful chunks, so the task can measure how expertise helps people reorganize the letter sequence.
It wipes out all effects of earlier letter sets, so any forgetting left over can be blamed purely on time-based decay.
It serves as the recall response itself, so memory for the letters is scored from how accurately participants count.
college.why: Counting backward blocks rehearsal of the letters during the delay. It does not remove interference from earlier trials, so forgetting cannot automatically be assigned to pure decay.

simple.stem: In the task used by Brown (1958) and Peterson and Peterson (1959), why did participants count backward by 3s?
options: To stop them from rehearsing the three letters during the delay.
To test how well they could do arithmetic under time pressure.
To help them group the three letters into one meaningful chunk.
To give them extra practice before recalling the three letters.
simple.why: Counting backward kept participants from rehearsing the letters, so the researchers could see how fast unrehearsed information is lost. It was not a test of arithmetic or a chunking aid.

college.stem: To separate a purely time-based explanation of forgetting in the task used by Brown (1958) and Peterson and Peterson (1959) from one involving built-up proactive interference, which comparison is most informative?
options: Compare recall after matched short and long delays on the first trial and on later trials, with the same counting task throughout.
Compare a group given an 18-second filled delay with a group given no delay at all, ignoring how many earlier trials each completed.
Compare early trials that use three letters with later trials that use six letters, so trial history and load change together.
Compare people who count backward during the delay with people allowed to repeat the letters, treating any gap as interference.
college.why: Matching delays across trial positions tests whether earlier trials matter, which pure decay does not predict. The other comparisons ignore trial history or change load or rehearsal along with it.

simple.stem: In the studies by Brown (1958) and Peterson and Peterson (1959), what did recall look like on the very first trial?
options: Recall was high after both the 3-second and 18-second delays.
Recall was high after 3 seconds but near zero after 18 seconds.
Recall was near zero after both the 3-second and 18-second delays.
Recall was much higher after 18 seconds than after 3 seconds.
simple.why: On the first trial, recall stayed high even after an 18-second delay. Poor recall at long delays appeared only after many trials, which points to interference from earlier letters.

college.stem: In the studies by Brown (1958) and Peterson and Peterson (1959), recall after a long delay was fairly high on the first trial but worse on later trials. Which conclusion is most defensible?
options: Earlier trials contribute to later forgetting, so the averaged delay curve cannot be read as evidence for time-based decay alone.
Time has no effect on any kind of memory, because a first-trial advantage disproves every account based on gradual loss over time.
The first trial produces permanent storage of every trigram, so later errors must come only from misunderstood instructions.
The averaged delay curve separates decay from interference, because averaging cancels the effects of earlier trials on memory.
college.why: The trial-position effect shows that earlier trigrams add to forgetting, so the averaged curve is not pure decay. It does not show that time never matters; forgetting in short-term memory involves both decay and interference.

simple.stem: What did Brown (1958) and Peterson and Peterson (1959) find about recall after long delays across a series of trials?
options: Recall after long delays got worse as the series of trials went on.
Recall after long delays got better as the series of trials went on.
Recall after long delays stayed the same on every trial in the series.
Recall after long delays was perfect on every trial after the first.
simple.why: Recall dropped with longer delays, but this depended on trial position: long-delay recall got worse as the series of trials got longer.

college.stem: A follow-up to Brown (1958) and Peterson and Peterson (1959) keeps the delay and counting task identical but compares people who have already studied many similar trigrams with people on their very first trigram. Which result supports proactive interference?
options: People with many earlier trigrams recall the current trigram less accurately than first-trial people at the same delay.
Both groups recall the current trigram equally well, but one group counts backward noticeably faster than the other.
First-trial people recall fewer letters, but only when given longer trigrams and a longer delay than the other group.
People forget an earlier trigram after studying a new one, while their recall of the new trigram stays unaffected.
college.why: Proactive interference is older information impairing recall of newer information, so prior trigrams should lower current recall at a matched delay. The last option describes the reverse direction, retroactive interference.

simple.stem: Brown (1958) and Peterson and Peterson (1959) set out to study decay. What other kind of forgetting did their results reveal?
options: Proactive interference, where older items make new items harder to recall.
Retroactive interference, where new items make older items harder to recall.
Sensory decay, where a visual icon fades in less than one second.
Procedural forgetting, where a practiced motor skill is slowly lost.
simple.why: Letters from earlier trials made it harder to recall the current letters, which is proactive interference. Retroactive interference runs the other way, with new information disrupting old.

college.stem: When newly learned information disrupts recall of older information, this is called ______, whereas older information disrupting recall of newer information is called ______.
options: retroactive interference in the first case and proactive interference in the second
proactive interference in the first case and retroactive interference in the second case
maintenance rehearsal in the first case and elaborative rehearsal in the second
encoding failure in the first case and sensory persistence in the second
college.why: Retroactive interference is new information disrupting old; proactive interference is old information disrupting new. Identify which memory is the target, not just which word comes first.

simple.stem: What is retroactive interference?
options: When new information makes it harder to remember old information.
When old information makes it harder to remember new information.
When information fades from memory just because time passes.
When information is repeated over and over to keep it active.
simple.why: Retroactive interference is a new memory interfering with remembering old information, such as a new phone number blocking the old one. Old information blocking new is proactive interference.

college.stem: A researcher defines digit span as the longest sequence a person recalls completely and in the correct order. Which procedure best matches that definition?
options: Present lists of increasing length and score a list as correct only when every digit is reproduced in its original order.
Present only four-digit lists and use the percentage of single digits recalled in any order as the person's longest span.
Present lists of increasing length and score a list as correct whenever its digits are recognized, even if their order is reversed.
Present one ten-digit list and estimate span from how long the person looks at it before beginning to respond.
college.why: The definition requires lists that grow in length and complete recall in order. Partial unordered recall, recognition, and looking time do not measure that.

simple.stem: How is a person's digit span measured?
options: By the longest row of digits they recall completely right, in order.
By the total number of digits they recall from all rows, in any order.
By how many seconds they can look at a row before forgetting it.
By how many digits they can recognize when shown them a second time.
simple.why: Digit span is the number of digits in the longest row recalled completely correctly. Counting scattered digits or recognition does not meet that rule.

college.stem: Which interpretation of Miller's (1956) “seven, plus or minus two” best fits later findings on visual capacity and chunking?
options: It counts capacity in items whose information content can vary, so it should not be applied as one fixed limit to every task.
It shows that exactly seven sensory features are stored in every modality, regardless of familiarity, organization, or complexity.
It states how many seconds every short-term trace lasts, so a visual estimate of four items measures the very same quantity.
It rules out any knowledge-based gains in span, since combining small items into meaningful groups cannot change performance.
college.why: What counts as one item matters: visual change-detection estimates are smaller, complex objects lower capacity, and chunking raises span. Capacity and duration are different quantities, so the third option confuses them.

simple.stem: What did Miller (1956) propose about short-term memory?
options: People can hold about seven, plus or minus two, items at once.
People can hold about three to four visual items at once.
People can hold information for about seven seconds without rehearsal.
People can hold an unlimited number of items for a short time.
simple.why: Miller (1956) proposed that people can remember about 7 ± 2 items, such as digits, words, or phrases. Three to four items is the later estimate for visual short-term memory from change detection.

college.stem: Following Alvarez and Cavanagh (2004), a researcher asks whether visual capacity depends on how complex each object is rather than on a fixed number of equivalent objects. Which design best answers this?
options: Compare change detection across matched set sizes for simple colored squares and complex objects, with timing and responses held constant.
Compare simple objects at small set sizes with complex objects at large set sizes, judging the effect of complexity from overall accuracy.
Compare immediate recognition of colored squares with delayed free recall of complex objects, treating any difference as due to complexity alone.
Present only one type of object and ask participants whether it looks complicated, without measuring retention or comparison accuracy.
college.why: Varying complexity while matching set size and task conditions isolates the effect of complexity. Changing set size, delay, or task type along with complexity leaves other explanations open.

simple.stem: What did Alvarez and Cavanagh (2004) use to study short-term memory capacity?
options: Change detection with colored squares and more complex objects.
Digit-span tests using rows of digits of increasing length.
Counting backward by threes between hearing letters and recall.
Chess positions shown briefly to masters and to beginners.
simple.why: Alvarez and Cavanagh (2004) used the change detection procedure with colored squares and more complex objects. Digit span, backward counting, and chess positions belong to other studies.

college.stem: A change-detection study finds accuracy falling sharply beyond about four colored squares, while digit-span tests allow more digits. How are these findings best reconciled?
options: The tasks differ in stimuli and demands, so a visual estimate of about three to four items need not match span for digits or words.
The visual result must be discarded, because Miller's (1956) proposal requires everyone to hold at least five objects in every task.
The digit-span result proves visual memory holds exactly the same number of objects, so the accuracy drop cannot reflect retention.
The visual result measures only how long rehearsal lasts, whereas digit span alone can estimate how much information is retained.
college.why: Visual short-term memory measured by change detection may have a smaller capacity than memory for lists of digits or words, and there may be several modality-specific forms of short-term memory. The visual task still measures retained information.

simple.stem: In change-detection studies of visual short-term memory, about how many items can people hold at once?
options: About three to four items before accuracy falls off sharply.
About seven, plus or minus two, items, as with digit lists.
About twelve items, the size of the largest display tested.
Only one item at a time, no matter how big the display is.
simple.why: Accuracy drops steeply with more than four items, suggesting a visual capacity of about three to four. Seven plus or minus two is Miller's estimate for items like digits and words.

college.stem: Two arrays each contain four objects: one has simple colored squares and the other complex shaded cubes. Someone argues that equal item counts mean equal memory demands. Which response best fits Alvarez and Cavanagh's (2004) change-detection findings?
options: Equal object counts need not mean equal information demands, since more complex objects lower change-detection performance.
Equal object counts guarantee equal demands, since the visual system treats every object as one identical item regardless of features.
Complex objects raise capacity, since their extra details give memory more independent storage slots to fill with information.
Any difference must come from different retention intervals, since complexity cannot affect performance when item count is fixed.
college.why: Same/different judgments depend on stimulus complexity: capacity is highest for colored squares and lowest for shaded cubes. Matching the number of objects does not match the amount of information to be held.

simple.stem: In a change-detection task like Alvarez and Cavanagh's (2004), two displays each have four items: one has colored squares, the other shaded cubes. Which display is easier to hold in visual short-term memory?
options: The colored squares, because simpler objects carry less information.
The shaded cubes, because complex objects stand out more clearly.
Both are equally easy, because each display has four items.
Neither can be held, because four items is beyond visual capacity.
simple.why: Visual capacity is higher for simple colored squares than for complex shaded cubes, so the squares are easier to hold. Item count alone does not set the memory load.

college.stem: Ericsson and colleagues (1980) trained a college student to reach a digit span of 79 by using familiar running times. Which explanation best separates this improvement from an unlimited increase in raw memory capacity?
options: Familiar knowledge let the digits be recoded into larger meaningful chunks, raising span without raising capacity for all kinds of information.
Training expanded each sensory store to hold 79 unrelated objects, so the same span should appear at once for unfamiliar visual patterns and words.
The student stopped relying on long-term knowledge, showing that meaningful organization adds nothing to an unusually high digit span.
The result shows that Miller's (1956) items must always be single digits, because trained and untrained people group digits identically.
college.why: The student chunked digits into meaningful running times from a sport he knew, which depends on long-term knowledge. Better span for this kind of information does not show a general expansion of every memory limit.

simple.stem: In Ericsson and colleagues' (1980) study, how did a college student reach a digit span of 79?
options: By chunking digits into meaningful running times, a sport he knew well.
By silently repeating every digit over and over until it was time to recall.
By having an unusually large short-term memory store from birth.
By counting backward by threes to block out other information.
simple.why: After training, the student chunked digits into meaningful running times. The gain came from chunking with existing knowledge, not from rehearsal or a naturally larger store.

college.stem: To test the chunking explanation of Chase and Simon's (1973) chess findings, which design and predicted pattern give the strongest evidence?
options: Compare masters and beginners on meaningful and random arrangements with matched piece counts; predict a master advantage mainly for meaningful ones.
Compare masters on meaningful positions with beginners on random positions; attribute any master advantage entirely to the masters' meaningful chunking.
Give masters more viewing time than beginners on meaningful positions; take higher master recall as evidence that viewing time is irrelevant.
Compare masters and beginners only on meaningful positions; conclude that any difference must come from familiarity with piece patterns.
college.why: Crossing expertise with arrangement type shows whether the master advantage depends on meaningful structure. The other designs confound group with arrangement or viewing time, or leave out the random condition needed for the test.

simple.stem: What did Chase and Simon (1973) find when chess masters and beginners recalled random piece arrangements?
options: Masters and beginners placed about the same number correctly.
Masters placed far more pieces correctly than the beginners did.
Beginners placed far more pieces correctly than the masters did.
Neither group was able to place any of the pieces correctly.
simple.why: With random arrangements, masters and beginners performed about the same. The masters' large advantage appeared only for meaningful game positions, which they could chunk.

college.stem: A learner arranges items along a familiar route (a “memory palace”) and deliberately shifts attention from one item to the next while recalling them. What do these strategies illustrate?
options: Control processes, which are active strategies a person uses to focus on and make information more memorable.
Purely passive storage, since directing attention and organizing information cannot change how memory is used.
Sensory persistence, since a remembered route stays physically visible to the learner throughout the learning.
Proactive interference, since the familiar route automatically blocks the new items from being remembered.
college.why: Control processes are active processes a person controls, including rehearsal, strategies that make a stimulus more memorable, and attention strategies. A memory palace and deliberate attention shifts are both of this kind.

simple.stem: In the modal model, what are control processes?
options: Active processes a person can control, such as rehearsal and attention.
Automatic processes that hold sensory copies for under a second.
Permanent stores that keep information for years or even decades.
Types of forgetting caused by old and new memories competing.
simple.why: Control processes are active processes the person controls, such as maintenance rehearsal, memory strategies, and attention strategies. They are not stores or types of forgetting.

college.stem: A person recalls a specific birthday party, knows that Paris is the capital of France, and can still ride a bicycle. How does the memory tree sort these three memories?
options: The party is episodic memory, the capital is semantic memory, and riding the bicycle is procedural memory.
The party is procedural memory, the capital is episodic memory, and riding the bicycle is semantic knowledge.
All three are sensory memories, because each one still influences how the person thinks or behaves now.
All three are short-term memories, because the person can bring each one of them to mind right now.
college.why: Personal events are episodic and facts are semantic (both declarative long-term memory), while skills are procedural. Being able to use a memory now does not make it a sensory or short-term store.

simple.stem: On the memory tree, which two types fall under declarative long-term memory?
options: Episodic memory for events and semantic memory for facts.
Procedural memory for skills and episodic memory for events.
Sensory memory for sights and short-term memory for numbers.
Procedural memory for skills and semantic memory for facts.
simple.why: Declarative long-term memory branches into episodic and semantic memory. Procedural memory is the other branch of long-term memory, and sensory and short-term memory are separate stores.

college.stem: After a bell stops ringing, its sound seems to linger for a moment; after a camera flash, an image of the scene briefly lingers too. Which pairing correctly names these two traces?
options: The lingering sound is an echo and the lingering image is an icon, both forms of sensory memory.
The lingering sound is an icon and the lingering image is an echo, both forms of sensory memory.
Both are procedural memories, since each one continues after the stimulation itself has ended.
Both are semantic memories, since their sensory sources are no longer present in the environment.
college.why: An echo is the brief continuation of a sound in the auditory system, and an icon is a fleeting visual image. Lingering after the stimulus ends does not make a trace a procedural skill or semantic knowledge.

simple.stem: What is an icon in sensory memory?
options: A fleeting mental image that lasts less than a second.
A brief continuation of a sound after it has ended.
A detailed picture memory that lasts for many years.
A meaningful symbol stored as a fact in long-term memory.
simple.why: An icon is a fleeting visual image held in sensory memory for less than a second. The continuation of a sound is an echo.

college.stem: In a modified version of Sperling's (1960) task, participants are told which row to memorize before the letter array appears. Why would high accuracy for that row say less about broad initial availability than a cue given after the array?
options: The advance cue lets participants focus on that row during exposure rather than drawing on an unknown row afterward.
The advance cue guarantees that participants register every row of the letter array with equal accuracy at the start.
The advance cue makes the letter array physically larger and adds to the number of letters actually displayed.
The advance cue removes any need for the letters to be registered visually before participants report them.
college.why: A cue after the display prevents participants from choosing in advance which row to encode. With an advance cue, accuracy for the cued row can come from focused attention without the other rows being retained.

simple.stem: In Sperling's (1960) partial report method, when did participants learn which row to report?
options: After the letters disappeared, when a tone signaled the row.
Before the letters appeared, when the row was named aloud.
While the letters were on screen, when the row lit up brightly.
They were never told and had to report every single row.
simple.why: In partial report, participants heard the tone only after viewing the letters, so they could not know in advance which row would be tested. Reporting every row is the whole report method.

college.stem: In Sperling's (1960) partial report method, accurate report is obtained no matter which row the tone signals. Why does the unpredictability of the cued row matter for interpreting this result?
options: Success on an unpredictable row means information from several rows was available before the tone picked out one.
Unpredictability means participants rehearse the cued row for a long while before the letter array is displayed.
Unpredictability shows that the entire letter array is stored permanently after every brief exposure to it.
Unpredictability means the number of letters recalled is the same in the whole and partial report conditions.
college.why: Since any row could be cued after the display and still be reported well, most of the array must have been available at that moment. This does not require advance rehearsal or permanent storage.

simple.stem: In Sperling's (1960) partial report method, why did it matter that participants could be asked to report any of the rows?
options: Doing well on any row meant letters from all rows were briefly available.
It let participants rehearse one chosen row before the display appeared.
It showed that all the letters were stored permanently in memory.
It made the partial report and whole report scores come out the same.
simple.why: Because participants could report any row well, letters from the whole display must have been briefly held in sensory memory. The cue came after the display, so no row could be rehearsed in advance.

college.stem: In Sperling's (1960) delayed partial report condition, the partial-report advantage shrinks as the tone is delayed while display time stays fixed. Which variable is changing the chance to select the requested letters?
options: The interval between the end of the letter display and the tone that signals the row.
The number of letters physically present in the display during the original exposure.
The length of time that the original letter display stays visible to the participant.
The sensory modality, visual or auditory, through which the letters themselves are delivered.
college.why: The delay changes when selection can happen after the same exposure. As it grows, the sensory trace fades before the row is identified, so the advantage shrinks.

simple.stem: In Sperling's (1960) results, about how long did it take for most of visual sensory memory to fade?
options: About one second after the display disappeared.
About 15 to 20 seconds after the display disappeared.
Several minutes after the display disappeared.
Several hours after the display disappeared.
simple.why: Within about one second, most of sensory memory decays, leaving only what attention moved into short-term memory. About 15 to 20 seconds is the effective duration of short-term memory.

college.stem: Someone argues that reporting four or five letters from a briefly flashed array measures exactly how many letters were registered at first. Which finding from Sperling (1960) shows this conclusion is incomplete?
options: An immediately cued partial report recovers most of whichever row is requested after the display ends.
A longer reporting period gives participants extra time to speak, even though the sensory trace keeps fading.
The complete array contains more than four or five printed letters before it is ever shown.
Participants already know that the letters are familiar symbols drawn from their own alphabet.
college.why: Accurate report of an unpredictable row shows that more was registered than whole report recovers. Whole report is limited because letters fade while they are being named.

simple.stem: Before Sperling (1960), many thought visual sensory memory held only 4–5 items. Which of his conditions showed this belief was incomplete?
options: The partial report condition, where people reported most letters of any cued row.
The whole report condition, where people reported about 4.5 letters in total.
A condition where people named the letters while they stayed on the screen.
A condition where people were told the row to report before the letters appeared.
simple.why: Partial report showed that most letters in any row were available, so the whole scene was encoded at first. Whole report produced the 4–5 item estimate; the last two conditions were not part of the study.

college.stem: A learner spends ten minutes on a new vocabulary word. In one session they repeat its definition aloud; in another they connect the word to a related word they already know well. Which difference does this contrast capture?
options: The second session uses elaborative rehearsal, while the first session relies mainly on maintenance rehearsal.
The first session uses elaborative rehearsal, because repetition automatically adds meaningful relationships.
Both sessions rely only on sensory memory, because the word itself is already quite familiar to the learner.
The second session blocks long-term learning, because it requires retrieving knowledge already in storage.
college.why: Connecting a word to existing knowledge is elaborative rehearsal; repeating it is maintenance rehearsal. Drawing on stored knowledge helps rather than blocks transfer to long-term memory.

simple.stem: Which strategy is a good way to transfer information from short-term memory into long-term memory?
options: Elaborative rehearsal, which links new information to existing knowledge.
Maintenance rehearsal, which repeats information silently over and over.
Counting backward by threes to keep other thoughts out of the way.
Letting the information sit in sensory memory for a little longer.
simple.why: Elaborative rehearsal links new information with existing knowledge in long-term memory and is a good way to transfer it there. Maintenance rehearsal only prolongs its presence in short-term memory.

college.stem: One group repeats a number throughout a delay, while another performs a task that prevents rehearsal. A researcher attributes any recall difference entirely to how long passive storage lasts. What else has this design changed?
options: Whether a control process is available to keep the information active during the delay.
The numerical values carried by each of the digits that make up the number.
The definition of duration, from elapsed time to the number of items remembered.
Whether the participants receive any information at all before they are asked to recall.
college.why: Rehearsal is a control process that extends duration, so allowing it in only one group changes what happens during the delay. The difference cannot be read as passive duration alone.

simple.stem: In short-term memory, which process seems to extend duration?
options: Rehearsal, which keeps repeating the information over time.
Chunking, which groups items into larger meaningful groups.
Interference, which lets old memories compete with new ones.
Decay, which lets the memory trace fade as time passes.
simple.why: Rehearsal seems to extend duration, while chunking seems to extend capacity. Interference and decay are causes of forgetting.

college.stem: In the procedure used by Brown (1958) and Peterson and Peterson (1959), participants count backward after receiving three letters. Which participant behavior would defeat the purpose of the retention interval?
options: Silently repeating the letters instead of keeping up the required backward counting.
Continuing the backward counting steadily until the signal to recall the letters.
Reporting the letters when the interval ends rather than while they are still visible.
Receiving filled delays of different lengths on different trials before recall.
college.why: Counting backward is meant to block rehearsal. Repeating the letters brings back the maintenance rehearsal the procedure is designed to prevent.

simple.stem: In the task used by Brown (1958) and Peterson and Peterson (1959), what were the steps in order?
options: Get three letters and a number, count backward by 3s for 3–18 seconds, then recall the letters.
Get three letters, repeat them aloud for 3–18 seconds in silence, then recall the letters.
Get a number, count forward by 3s, see three letters, then recall the original number.
Get three letters and a number, recall the letters at once, then count backward by 3s.
simple.why: Participants received three letters and a number, counted backward by 3s during a 3–18 second delay, and then recalled the letters. Repeating the letters would have allowed rehearsal, which the task was built to prevent.

college.stem: In the studies by Brown (1958) and Peterson and Peterson (1959), long-delay recall is good on the first trial but worse after several earlier trials. Which comparison is needed to attribute this difference to trial history rather than to different retention times?
options: Compare early and later trials at the same delay, using the same rehearsal-blocking counting task.
Compare an early short-delay trial with a later long-delay trial while also changing the counting task.
Compare one participant copying visible letters with another participant recalling absent letters.
Compare only the overall average across all delays, setting aside the order in which trials occurred.
college.why: Holding delay and the counting task constant isolates the effect of earlier trials. Changing delay or task, or letting the letters stay visible, adds other explanations, and averaging hides trial order.

simple.stem: Why did recall after long delays get worse over a series of trials in the studies by Brown (1958) and Peterson and Peterson (1959)?
options: Letters from earlier trials interfered with remembering the new letters.
Participants grew better at counting backward as the trials went on.
New letters pushed the earliest letters out of long-term memory.
The delays before recall got much shorter as the trials went on.
simple.why: The pattern reflects proactive interference: letters already learned on earlier trials made the new letters harder to recall.

college.stem: In the studies by Brown (1958) and Peterson and Peterson (1959), the recall curve averaged over all trials declines with delay, but it combines first trials with later ones. Which conclusion takes the trial pattern into account?
options: The average mixes trials with different amounts of built-up interference, so trial position also shapes the explanation.
The average proves that every participant loses the same number of letters on every trial, purely because time passes.
Averaging removes interference from the data, leaving a clean estimate of how passive decay unfolds over time.
Having an average means that recall on the first trial cannot differ from recall on later trials.
college.why: Later trials carry interference from earlier trigrams, and an average can hide that difference rather than remove it. Forgetting in short-term memory involves both decay and interference.

simple.stem: When results were averaged over all trials in the studies by Brown (1958) and Peterson and Peterson (1959), what pattern appeared?
options: Recall was much lower after an 18-second delay than after 3 seconds.
Recall was about the same after the 3-second and 18-second delays.
Recall was much higher after an 18-second delay than after 3 seconds.
Recall was close to zero after both the 3-second and 18-second delays.
simple.why: Averaged over all trials, recall dropped sharply from the 3-second to the 18-second delay. Looking trial by trial showed the drop grew as the series went on.

college.stem: After switching to a new phone number, a person has trouble recalling their old one. Which kind of interference does this show?
options: Retroactive interference, because newer information is disrupting memory for older information.
Proactive interference, because any interference involving a new number receives that label.
Sensory persistence, because the old number is still physically in view for the person.
Elaborative rehearsal, because the two numbers have been permanently merged into one memory.
college.why: The target is the old number and the interfering information is newer, which defines retroactive interference. Proactive interference runs the other way, with old information disrupting new.

simple.stem: You get a new locker combination and now can't remember your old one. What is this?
options: Retroactive interference, where new information blocks old.
Proactive interference, where old information blocks new information.
Decay, where the old memory simply faded away with time.
Chunking, where the two combinations merged into one memory.
simple.why: A new memory interfering with an old one is retroactive interference. Proactive interference would be the old combination making the new one hard to remember.

college.stem: A commuter parks in a different spot in the same campus lot every weekday. On Friday afternoon, they keep recalling Thursday's spot instead of Friday's. Which account identifies the target memory and the interference?
options: Friday's spot is the target memory, and the older spots from earlier days produce proactive interference.
Thursday's spot is the target memory, and the newer spot from Friday produces retroactive interference.
Friday's spot is the target memory, and sensory persistence keeps the older spots permanently in view.
Parking is a procedural skill, so the order in which the spots were learned does not matter at all.
college.why: The commuter wants the newer memory, and older similar memories compete with it, which is proactive interference. Routine events like daily parking are especially prone to this.

simple.stem: Proactive and retroactive interference are worst for which kind of events?
options: Routine events that happen in much the same way again and again.
Unusual events that happen only once and stand out from the rest.
Emotional events that happened long ago in early childhood.
Events that happened less than one second ago.
simple.why: Both kinds of interference are worst for routine events. Unusual events are less prone to interference.

college.stem: Interference theories hold that forgetting comes from memories competing, not from the mere passage of time. Which statement correctly contrasts retroactive and proactive interference?
options: In retroactive interference new information disrupts old; in proactive interference old information disrupts new.
In retroactive interference old information disrupts new; in proactive interference new information disrupts old.
In retroactive interference longer rehearsal helps recall; in proactive interference shorter rehearsal helps recall.
In retroactive interference visual traces turn auditory; in proactive interference auditory traces turn visual.
college.why: The two types differ in whether the competing memory came after or before the target memory. They are not about rehearsal length or sensory modality.

simple.stem: In interference theories, what causes forgetting?
options: One memory competing with or replacing another memory.
The mere passage of time causing the memory to fade.
Damage to the brain areas that store older memories.
Repeating information too many times during rehearsal.
simple.why: Interference theories say forgetting is caused by one memory competing with or replacing another, not by the mere passage of time.

college.stem: A participant reproduces every digit of an eight-digit sequence but reverses two of them, after reproducing a seven-digit sequence perfectly in order. Under standard digit-span scoring, which interpretation is correct?
options: The eight-digit trial counts as wrong under ordered scoring, so recalling its digits does not give a span of eight.
The eight-digit trial counts as correct, because only the identity of the digits matters and their order is ignored.
The participant has demonstrated an unlimited span, because every single digit in both of the sequences is a familiar symbol.
The seven-digit trial cannot count, because shorter sequences never contribute anything to a span estimate.
college.why: Digit span is the longest row recalled completely correctly, which requires the right order. Getting the digits without the order does not make the eight-digit row correct, so the span here is seven.

simple.stem: Maria recalls the 6-digit row perfectly but mixes up two digits in the 7-digit row. What is her digit span?
options: Six, since that is her longest row recalled completely right.
Seven, since she remembered all the digits in that row.
Thirteen, since that is the total number of digits in both rows.
Zero, since she made at least one mistake somewhere overall.
simple.why: Digit span is the number of digits in the longest row recalled completely correctly. The 7-digit row had an error, so her span is six.

college.stem: Miller's (1956) estimate of seven, plus or minus two, is compared with a visual change-detection estimate of about three or four items. Which interpretation is most defensible?
options: The estimates come from different tasks and kinds of items, so one number should not be applied to every measure.
The visual result is impossible, because Miller established a limit of exactly seven raw elements in every memory task.
The digit estimate measures visual sensory persistence, while every visual task measures permanent long-term storage.
The two estimates must be averaged together to obtain the single correct capacity that applies to every participant and every kind of task.
college.why: Visual short-term memory measured by change detection may have a smaller capacity than memory for digits or words, and theorists debate how many specific forms of short-term memory exist. Neither estimate is sensory persistence or permanent storage.

simple.stem: How does visual short-term memory capacity from change detection compare with Miller's (1956) 7 ± 2?
options: It is smaller, about three to four items, than for digit lists.
It is larger, about twelve items, than memory for digit lists.
It is exactly the same, about seven items, as for digit lists.
It cannot be measured at all, because visual items fade too fast.
simple.why: Change detection suggests visual short-term memory holds about three to four items, smaller than the 7 ± 2 estimate for digits or words.

college.stem: A visual change-detection task shows display S1 for 100 ms, removes it for 900 ms, and then shows display S2. Which change would make the task a weaker test of short-term visual retention?
options: Keeping S1 on screen beside S2, so participants can compare the two displays directly.
Removing S1 before S2 appears and requiring a same-or-different judgment about them.
Holding the exposure time of S1 constant while comparing displays of different sizes.
Using the same relevant visual features, such as color, in both the first and second displays.
college.why: If both displays are visible together, participants can compare them by looking rather than by holding S1 in memory. The original task requires keeping S1 in mind across the blank gap.

simple.stem: In a change-detection task, what does the participant do?
options: Sees a display, then after a gap judges if a second display is the same.
Sees a display and then names every item in it aloud from memory.
Sees two displays side by side and points out every difference between the two of them.
Hears a row of digits and repeats them back in the original order.
simple.why: In change detection, a first display is shown briefly, removed, and followed by a second display; the participant judges same or different. Repeating digits in order is a digit-span task.

college.stem: Change-detection accuracy falls sharply as display size grows beyond about four colored squares. What is the most appropriate interpretation for visual short-term memory?
options: Holding the needed visual information becomes less successful once the display exceeds a limited capacity.
All objects are retained permanently, and larger displays remove any need to compare the two displays.
Participants lose the ability to see any of the colors once a display contains more than four separate items.
Every kind of short-term memory task must have exactly the same limit of four items as this one.
college.why: The drop reflects limited visual short-term memory, about three to four items. It does not mean participants cannot see the colors, that storage is permanent, or that every task has the same limit.

simple.stem: In change-detection studies, what happened to accuracy when displays had more than four items?
options: Accuracy dropped off sharply as more items were added.
Accuracy stayed near perfect no matter how many items there were.
Accuracy rose steadily as more and more items were added.
Accuracy fell to zero as soon as a fifth item appeared.
simple.why: Accuracy fell off dramatically beyond four items, suggesting people can hold only about three to four items in visual short-term memory. It dropped but did not reach zero.

college.stem: Alvarez and Cavanagh (2004) compared change detection for simple colored squares and more complex objects such as shaded cubes. Which result supports measuring capacity by amount of information rather than by number of items?
options: Estimated capacity was higher for simple colored squares than for complex objects such as shaded cubes.
Every object category gave exactly the same capacity estimate, whatever visual features had to be retained.
Participants named every object while both displays stayed visible on the screen with no delay.
The verbal label for an object set its capacity even when its visual features were never tested.
college.why: Complex objects carry more information, and capacity was lower for them than for colored squares. If every item counted equally, capacity would not vary by object type.

simple.stem: What did Alvarez and Cavanagh (2004) find about object complexity and visual short-term memory?
options: The more complex the objects, the fewer could be held in memory.
The more complex the objects, the more could be held in memory.
Object complexity had no effect on how many could be held in memory.
Only colored squares could be held; complex objects could not be held at all.
simple.why: Capacity was highest for colored squares and lowest for shaded cubes, so complex objects reduced how many could be held. Complex objects still had a capacity above zero.

college.stem: A researcher wants to test, in the manner of Alvarez and Cavanagh (2004), whether stimulus complexity affects visual-memory capacity. Which comparison most directly does this?
options: Compare change detection for simple and complex objects while keeping exposure, delay, and response demands comparable.
Compare simple objects shown for a long time with complex objects shown briefly, and change the response instructions too.
Ask one group to remember digits and another group to report whether the testing room is brightly lit.
Keep complex objects visible throughout the response and compare them with simple objects that are removed.
college.why: The relevant manipulation is object complexity under the same memory demands. Changing exposure, instructions, or visibility along with complexity creates other explanations.

simple.stem: In Alvarez and Cavanagh's (2004) study, which kind of object had the lowest capacity?
options: Shaded cubes, the most complex objects that were tested.
Colored squares, the simplest objects that were tested.
Chinese characters, the written symbols that were tested.
Random polygons, the irregular shapes that were tested.
simple.why: Capacity was lowest for shaded cubes (under two items) and highest for colored squares (over four). Chinese characters and random polygons fell in between.

college.stem: Ericsson and colleagues (1980) trained a student to reach a very large digit span using familiar running times. What is the basis of this gain?
options: Knowledge-based chunking, which combines smaller units into larger meaningful units the student could hold.
A growth in raw storage capacity that becomes equally unlimited for every unfamiliar kind of information.
Replacing all long-term knowledge with a brief, unstructured sensory trace of the digits exactly as they appeared.
Doing away with any representation of the original sequence when recalling the digits in order.
college.why: Familiar running times let the student combine digits into larger meaningful chunks. This is chunking with existing knowledge, not a general expansion of every basic memory limit.

simple.stem: What is chunking?
options: Combining smaller units into larger meaningful units to hold more in memory.
Repeating information over and over to keep it in short-term memory.
Breaking a memory into pieces so that it can be forgotten more easily.
Moving information from sensory memory straight into long-term memory.
simple.why: Chunking is combining smaller units into larger meaningful units, which lets more fit in short-term memory. Repeating information is maintenance rehearsal.

college.stem: Chase and Simon (1973) compared chess masters and beginners recalling meaningful game positions and randomized positions. Which pattern supports expertise-based chunking?
options: Masters had a large advantage for meaningful positions, which disappeared for random arrangements.
Masters showed the same large advantage for random positions, regardless of any familiar relationships among pieces.
Beginners outperformed masters, but only when both groups copied the pieces while the board stayed visible.
Randomizing positions improved masters' recall, because familiar structure normally interferes with their memory.
college.why: Masters use learned chunks from meaningful positions. Random arrangements keep the pieces but destroy the familiar patterns, and the masters' advantage vanished.

simple.stem: What did Chase and Simon (1973) find when chess masters and beginners recalled pieces from meaningful game positions?
options: Masters placed many more pieces correctly than beginners.
Masters and beginners placed about the same number correctly.
Beginners placed many more pieces correctly than masters.
Neither group could place more than one or two pieces.
simple.why: For meaningful positions, masters placed far more pieces correctly because they chunk the board into meaningful patterns. This advantage did not appear for random arrangements.

college.stem: In Chase and Simon's (1973) study, why are random chess arrangements useful for evaluating the claim that masters simply have a larger raw visual store?
options: They keep the same kinds of pieces but break up the familiar patterns that support expert chunks.
They allow the masters to rehearse meaningful positions for a longer time than the beginners can.
They remove all visual information from the board and turn the task into a form of auditory recall.
They guarantee that both groups know the same number of chess strategies before the test begins.
college.why: If masters simply had a bigger raw store, they should excel with random arrangements too. Their advantage disappearing for random boards shows it depends on meaningful structure.

simple.stem: Why did Chase and Simon (1973) also test random chess arrangements?
options: To see if masters' advantage depended on meaningful patterns.
To give the beginners more time to study the chess pieces.
To check whether masters could see the board more clearly.
To find out how many chess rules each beginner already knew well.
simple.why: Random arrangements remove the meaningful patterns masters can chunk. Because masters lost their advantage, their skill came from chunking, not a bigger memory store.

college.stem: A learner groups a long sequence into meaningful units and also keeps repeating those units during a delay. Which pairing correctly distinguishes what each control process contributes?
options: Chunking packs more into each item held, while rehearsal prolongs how long the units stay available.
Chunking measures how much time has passed, while rehearsal permanently removes all capacity limits.
Both processes show that sensory memory retains every original detail of the sequence indefinitely.
Rehearsal changes the physical input itself, while chunking stops long-term knowledge from contributing.
college.why: Chunking seems to extend capacity by organizing information, and rehearsal seems to extend duration by maintaining it. Neither implies unlimited storage or lasting sensory traces.

simple.stem: To remember 1-9-9-4-2-0-2-6, you group it as the years 1994 and 2026 and keep repeating them. What are you doing?
options: Chunking to fit more in memory, and rehearsal to keep it there longer.
Rehearsal to fit more in memory, and chunking to keep it there longer.
Using sensory memory to hold an exact copy for many minutes.
Using proactive interference to block out the earlier digits.
simple.why: Grouping digits into meaningful years is chunking, which extends capacity; repeating them is rehearsal, which extends duration. The second option swaps their roles.

college.stem: A person pictures a familiar house and places each item to be remembered in a different room, then deliberately directs attention to each room while recalling. Which concept covers these active operations?
options: Control processes, which a person uses to organize and manage information being remembered.
A view of temporary memory as purely passive storage that no strategy is able to influence.
An automatic guarantee that every sensory detail of the house and its rooms will enter permanent memory.
Retroactive interference, which applies whenever information is tied to a spatial layout.
college.why: The memory palace is a strategy for making information more memorable, and directing attention is an attention strategy; both are control processes. They concern how information is managed, not passive retention.

simple.stem: Building a “memory palace” is an ancient strategy for making information more memorable. What kind of process is it?
options: A control process that the person actively chooses to use.
An automatic sensory process that the person cannot control.
A kind of retroactive interference between new and old items.
A form of decay that happens as more time passes.
simple.why: A memory palace is a strategy the person chooses, making it a control process. Control processes include rehearsal, memory strategies, and attention strategies.
